title: Your First Prioritization Frameworks
description: Learn the basics of RICE, ICE, and MoSCoW to make better decisions about what to work on first.

interactions.prompt: What does the 'R' in the RICE scoring framework stand for?

options.text: Reach
Revenue
Risk
Return

interactions.teachingPreamble: RICE is a popular prioritization framework created at Intercom. It scores projects on four factors: Reach (how many people it affects), Impact (how much it affects them), Confidence (how sure you are), and Effort (how much work it takes). The final score is (Reach × Impact × Confidence) ÷ Effort.

interactions.prompt: Project A: Reach 500, Impact 3, Confidence 80%, Effort 2. Project B: Reach 2000, Impact 2, Confidence 50%, Effort 4. Which project has the higher RICE score?

options.text: Project A (RICE score: 600)
Project B (RICE score: 500)
They are tied at 500
Cannot calculate without more data

interactions.prompt: How does MoSCoW differ from RICE in its approach to prioritization?

options.text: It uses numerical scores on a 1-10 scale
It sorts items into four priority categories
It focuses only on financial return
It requires a full cost-benefit analysis

interactions.teachingPreamble: MoSCoW is a simpler framework often used in product and project management. It groups items into four buckets: Must have (non-negotiable), Should have (important but not critical), Could have (nice to have), and Won't have (not now). Spotify uses MoSCoW-style thinking to define what goes into each product release.

interactions.prompt: In the ICE framework, a project is scored by multiplying its Impact, Confidence, and ____ on a scale of 1-10.

options.text: Effort
Ease
Efficiency
Execution

interactions.prompt: You're a PM at Shopify with one sprint left before launch. Feature X is a 'Should have' that 60% of beta users requested. Feature Y is a 'Must have' with a known bug fix. Which do you prioritize?

options.text: Feature X — user demand is the strongest signal
Feature Y — Must haves always come before Should haves
Split the sprint 50/50 between both features
Delay launch to ship both features fully

interactions.prompt: Why is 'Cost of Delay' a powerful addition to basic prioritization frameworks?

options.text: It replaces the need for any scoring framework
It quantifies what you lose by not acting now
It only applies to financial projects
It eliminates the need for stakeholder input

interactions.teachingPreamble: Cost of Delay asks: 'What do we lose for every week we don't ship this?' Amazon famously uses this thinking — if a checkout improvement generates $200K/week, delaying it by 3 weeks costs $600K. This reframes prioritization from 'what's most valuable' to 'what's most urgent to capture value now.'

interactions.prompt: Using Cost of Delay thinking, rank these projects from highest to lowest priority: (a) New dashboard — saves team 2hrs/week, no deadline. (b) Compliance fix — $50K/day fine starts in 5 days. (c) Onboarding flow — losing 30% of signups daily. (d) Logo redesign — brand refresh planned for next quarter.

options.text: New dashboard — saves 2hrs/week
Compliance fix — $50K/day fine imminent
Onboarding flow — losing 30% of signups daily
Logo redesign — planned for next quarter

interactions.prompt: Your CEO just announced the company is pivoting to enterprise sales starting next month. The logo redesign is now part of a critical enterprise pitch deck due in 10 days. How does your priority ranking change?

options.text: Logo redesign jumps up — its cost of delay just skyrocketed
No change — compliance and onboarding still matter more
Drop everything and focus only on the logo redesign
Delay the enterprise pivot until other projects finish

interactions.priorContext: Previously, the logo redesign ranked last because it had low cost of delay — it was a nice-to-have planned for next quarter. Now the context has shifted: a strategic pivot makes it time-sensitive with real revenue implications.
